webTitle: Morning Mail: Australians among hundreds caught in deadly Nepal floods, Meta settles landmark lawsuit, Tim Curry dies

fields.headline: Morning Mail: Australians among hundreds caught in deadly Nepal floods, Meta settles landmark lawsuit, Tim Curry dies
fields.trailText: At least 157 dead in Himalayan disaster; residents in Tasmania angry at planned AI datacentre
fields.bodyText: Good morning. More than 150 people are dead and hundreds more are missing – including a reported 34 Australian tourists – after a flash flood swept away houses, roads and bridges on the Nepal-Tibet border. Residents in Tasmania are angry at the planning process around a datacentre, while our economics columnist wonders if it’s worth building them at all, and could they cost Donald Trump the midterms? Plus: Meta settles a landmark lawsuit with US states over harm to children, and the Rocky Horror star Tim Curry has died. Australia Icac denial | The sister-in-law of former Liberal NSW premier Dominic Perrottet has told the state Icac hearing that she rejected the suggestion that she had been put in an “impossible situation” and lied under oath to cover illegal donations to her husband, an inquiry has heard. Datacentre debate | As Anthony Albanese endured a tough day wrangling the issue of datacentres at national cabinet, people in northern Tasmania were still seething after their local council approved a new facility that they say threatens to use excessive water and energy. Health saving | Removing the higher private health insurance rebate for people aged 65 and over is good policy that is unlikely to place additional pressure on public hospitals, according to health economists. Comic cut | The Egyptian-American comedian Bassem Youssef has announced his imminent Australian tour has been postponed after he was asked to provide background checks as part of his visa application. Royal commission | From the initial rumpus over Dennis Richardson to victims sharing their anguish, Ben Doherty picks key moments from the four months of the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion. World Himalayan disaster | At least 157 people have died and hundreds are missing after flash floods ⁠hit the Himalayan border areas of ⁠Nepal and Tibet. Many of the missing are overseas tourists, including at least 33 Britons and 34 Australians (by one early estimate). Meta settles | Meta reached an agreement of up to US$18bn to settle a landmark case brought by states across the US that accused the tech giant of addicting and harming children with dangerous products, according to a court filing. Dementia clue | Women using hormone replacement therapy are at lower risk of dementia, a new study suggests, with scientists finding those who had used HRT were 10% less likely to be diagnosed with the condition. ‘Escape wizard’ | Police in Spain have arrested a dangerous Albanian criminal nicknamed the “escape wizard” who has managed to break out of four jails in Italy and Belgium. Tim Curry tributes | Tim Curry, the versatile performer of screen and stage, who made his name as the flamboyant Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Show, has died aged 80. Our chief film critic pays tribute to Curry’s subversive blast of fun. Full Story Decoding America: Could datacentres lose Trump the midterms? Co-hosts Jonathan Yerushalmy and Reged Ahmad explore why datacentres in the US have provoked such anger – and whether that could harm Republicans in the midterms. In-depth The millions of dollars being invested in datacentres does not impress Greg Jericho. He explains in his column why it’s unlikely to lift living standards for Australians, isn’t showing up as any meaningful construction industry boost, and could also provoke another rate rise. Meanwhile fears are rising that the Reserve Bank will hit millions of mortgage holders with a fourth rate hike this year due to stubbornly high inflation. Not the news Does anyone need to spend $1,000 on a pillow? Thaslima Begum went in search of the perfect sleep and found that slumbering bliss comes at a price. Sport Tennis | On the eve of what she hopes will be a US Open challenge, Amanda Anisimova talks about learning to cope with the stresses of the tour and bouncing back. Football | Uefa is poised to drop its threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after receiving guarantees that the global governing body will never attempt a repeat of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup. A winner of that tournament, Emiliano Martínez, could be leaving Aston Villa for Chelsea, and there’s Carabao Cup action in England this morning. Cricket | Joe Root’s “robust conversation” with the England Test squad at Lord’s this week has finally ended any uncertainty about the conduct expected of them, according to fast bowler Josh Tongue. Media roundup The Australian claims that Labor will soon reveal its plans for immigration levels, with restrictions expected on international students and onshore visa applications. The WA government is appealing the landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, WAtoday reports, seeking “clarity” on the $150m judgment. The Broncos star Reece Walsh faces sanction by the club after liking a post that criticised the coach, the Courier Mail reports. What’s happening today Business | Wesfarmers, Star Entertainment Group and Qantas release full year results. Sydney | Full federal court appeal hearing by retired judge Walter Sofronoff over finding of corrupt conduct in Bruce Lehrmann inquiry. Darwin | Reforms to legalise voluntary assistant dying expected to be debated in the Northern Territory parliament. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland. Brain teaser And finally, here are the Guardian’s crosswords to keep you entertained throughout the day. webTitle: How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks

fields.headline: How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks
fields.trailText: The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans
fields.bodyText: Earlier this year, a survey found that Canada, along with Switzerland, was the best-liked country in the world. We all know this kind of polling is about as scientific as a high school popularity contest, but at least anecdotally, Canadians have a reputation for being friendly and welcoming, respectful and polite. Many people would find it difficult to dislike Canadians. But not Donald Trump, who in a “hold my beer” moment this week demonstrated that he, at least, finds it easy to resent Canadians. The US president called the country “difficult and unreasonable”, and in a particularly hysterical moment, threatened to rename a lake, after trade talks collapsed. Days earlier, Trump had claimed a deal with Canada was imminent, which would avoid the new taxes. But, in a development that surely galled the Art of the Deal author, there was no agreement. Instead, Trump and his team demonstrated the art of collapsing the deal, as trade talks fell apart due to what Canada said were unreasonable, last-minute demands from the US side. It meant that the US tariffs duly came in on Saturday, applied to various Canadian exports including hockey sticks and tongue depressors, but if Trump expected Canada to bow to his demands – the president was seeking more favorable terms on things like steel and aluminum – he was disappointed. Instead, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who has emerged as a rare world leader willing to stand up to Trump, said Canada had been “attacked”, and announced retaliatory tariffs on about $20bn worth of US goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment. All this means US consumers are seeing surging prices on all kinds of products – including toilet paper. My colleague Lauren Aratani reports that “the US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population”. And this outsize usage has grown more expensive. “Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials,” she writes. It’s fair to say that Canada’s retaliation upset Trump, who famously loves to win. On Tuesday, he claimed the US “is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer” – we’ll see how that goes – and has dubbed Canadian negotiators “clowns”. Earlier this week, Trump compared Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, unfavorably to his deceased brother Rob, the scandal-plagued former mayor of Toronto, whose time in office saw him admit to smoking crack cocaine and being “hammered” in public. And while Trump was flailing about, JD Vance was doing his best Scrappy-Doo, “lemme at ’em” impression, lobbing insults at Canada from the safety of a Republican rally in Maine. Vance claimed that Canada and China are “the two worst countries when it comes to trade policy anywhere in the world”. He added: “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry. Freudian slip. That was actually an accident.” The satisfied look on his face didn’t make it seem like one. Vance went on to add that Canada “quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. It was an interesting take, given the only country that has mused about invading Canada is the US – as recently as last year Trump was threatening to annex the nation. So in a nutshell: Donald Trump has led the US into an unsavory spat against the world’s most popular country, a scrap that could result in Americans – less than three months out from crucial midterm elections in which Republicans face an uphill battle – struggle to pay for a roll of toilet paper. Win!

webTitle: Three pro-Israel Democrats given key roles on House foreign affairs panel

fields.headline: Three pro-Israel Democrats given key roles on House foreign affairs panel
fields.trailText: Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Wesley Bell to join as Jared Moskowitz becomes ranking member on subcommittee
fields.bodyText: Three pro-Israel Democrats have been given key roles on a powerful congressional body overseeing US foreign policy in a move running sharply counter to popular sentiment within the party and likely to anger leftwing activists. The appointments to the US House of Representatives foreign affairs committee follow a succession of wins in party primaries for progressive candidates who put criticism of Israel and its actions in Gaza at the core of their campaign messages. In an apparent effort to stem the anti-Israeli tide, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, a representative from Florida, and the Missouri representative Wesley Bell will join the committee, while Jared Moskowitz, also from Florida, becomes the Democrats’ ranking member on the subcommittee for the Middle East and North Africa. All three recently defeated primary challengers who targeted them for their pro-Israel positions. Mark Pocan, a progressive Democrat from Wisconsin who has vocally criticised the powerful American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or Aipac, also joins the committee. Moskowitz, who last week defeated an anti-Zionist democratic socialist challenger, Oliver Larkin, vowed to use his new position to advance support for Israel. “At a moment of enormous change across the region, I’ll work to strengthen America’s relationships with Israel and our Gulf allies, expand regional peace, advance American diplomacy, and ensure our foreign policy is grounded in strength, security, and reality. I’m ready to get to work,” he posted on social media. He predicted his position would become vital if the Democrats retake the House in November’s midterm elections, as many polls indicate. “If Democrats take control of the House, I’ll be in a position to help steer US policy on Israel and the Middle East,” Moskowitz told Axios. In a statement on Wednesday, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair) expressed “deep concern” with the appointments of three Democrats whom it described as being among “the Israeli government’s most committed and consistent enablers”. Their elevation was an “insult to American voters and a desperate attempt to shield the Israeli government from accountability”, said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, the group’s national deputy director. “These decisions must not stand.” In this month’s primary campaign, Moskowitz accused Larkin, his opponent, of antisemitism and refused to debate him. One rabbi reportedly urged Republican congregants to register as Democrats in order to vote for Moskowitz. Wasserman Schultz won her primary after her congressional district was heavily redrawn, beating her main challenger, 27-year-old Elijah Manley, who also criticised her support for Israel and acceptance of financial donations from Aipac. Bell won a rematch poll against the former Democratic representative Cori Bush, who he defeated in a 2024 primary. Bush was a vocal critic of Israel’s military offensive in Gaza. Polls consistently show a loss of support for Israel among a US electorate that once staunchly backed it. The drop in support is particularly pronounced among younger voters, with older Republicans and white evangelicals being the only groups showing majorities holding favorable views of Israel, according to a Pew Poll in April. A leftwing Democrat, Angie Nixon – a vocal critic of Israel – last week won a special election to become the party’s Senate candidate in Florida in November.

webTitle: This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November | Robert Reich

fields.headline: This is the question Democrats should ask voters in order to win this November
fields.trailText: They should ask the question Reagan asked at the end of his debate against Jimmy Carter: ‘Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?’
fields.bodyText: The midterm elections are already upon us, and every Democrat and independent running against a Republican should ask voters the question Ronald Reagan asked on 28 October 1980, at the end of his televised debate against Jimmy Carter: “Are you better off now than you were before this presidency?” Unless you’re very, very rich, the answer is obviously: “No, I’m worse off.” Start with his tariffs, which are costing every American household an average of $1,100 annually, according to the Yale Budget Lab. (If you don’t trust Yale, the conservative Tax Foundation estimated last year’s tab to be $1,000 a household.) Even cleaning supplies and toilet paper are up at least 5%. Household furnishings, up at least 8%. Clothing, up at least 14%. Trump’s tariffs have also increased the costs of big-ticket items such as cars and made it more expensive to build new homes. Other studies find that the tariffs have added as much as 0.7 and 0.5 percentage points to the consumer price index and the personal consumption expenditures price index, respectively. Then there’s Trump’s war in Iran, which is driving up energy and food prices, as oil tankers remain stranded in the strait of Hormuz. The war is costing more at the gas pump – about $670 more a household since the war began. Americans face what the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers describe as “a worsening utility debt crisis”. The groups wrote in an analysis published last month: Energy bills have increased three times faster than the rate of inflation while Trump has been president. The national average monthly utility bill reached $280 in early 2026, a 12% increase since the end of 2024, just before the second Trump administration took office. What’s the Republican response to soaring energy utility prices? Eliminate billions in clean energy subsidies and tilt the scales toward costlier, dirtier fossil fuels. Also driving up the cost of electricity are AI datacenters. They’re also using up huge amounts of water and creating noise pollution. And who’s been pushing these datacenters? Trump and, before recent backlash, many Republicans. Trump’s war and the blockage of the strait are also causing fertilizer shortages, which are sending food prices upward. Millions of Americans are now struggling to afford groceries. Meanwhile, Trump’s huge tax cuts – which mostly benefited big corporations and the super-wealthy – are being paid for, in part, by Republican cuts to Medicaid and Medicare. Trump announced last month that he is ending Medicare subsidies that have kept drug prices low for seniors; Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act have deprived millions of Americans of health insurance. Hell, even Trump’s executive order to divide the measles, mumps, rubella vaccine into three shots instead of one is adding burdens to the typical American family. As the Republican senator Bill Cassidy said on ABC’s This Week: “This is why the president’s poll numbers are down, because you’ve lost sight of affordability for the parent. You’ve lost sight of the convenience for the American family. You’ve lost sight of that which is driving higher costs in healthcare – for example, more doctor’s visits … for something which has no rationale in science.” Trump’s obsession with gutting the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has denied Americans billions in foregone rebates and settlements. The regime spent $464m of taxpayer dollars in a no-bid contract for a special fleet of jets intended to deport immigrants. The planes have almost never been used. On and on it goes. Trump says the US economy is “doing unbelievably from the standpoint of Wall Street”. Maybe, but most Americans live on Main Street and own few if any shares of stock. The richest 1% holds more than half of the value of stocks listed on US stock exchanges; the richest 10%, 92%. Even including retirement accounts, only 16% of adult Americans have assets exceeding $100,000. The stock market boom reflects a boom in corporate profits. The pharmaceutical industry, big oil, and other sectors are posting banner earnings. Second quarter earnings for S&P 500 companies are on pace to rise a remarkable 50% year over year, the highest growth rate since the second quarter of 2021. But average working Americans are struggling to keep their heads above water. Trump’s comments about the roaring stock market came the same day that new data showed US consumer sentiment dropped in August. Americans’ outlook on the country’s economic conditions have worsened among Republicans as well as among Democrats. The July jobs report showed the US economy shedding 23,000 jobs, wage growth slowing, and the unemployment rate falling because more people left the workforce. My humble advice to Democratic candidates in the midterms: don’t be distracted. Don’t take the bait and discuss socialism, “wokeism”, or anything else. Just ask this simple question: are you better off now than you were before this presidency? And explain how badly Trump and congressional Republicans have shafted average working people. You’re better off than you were before the start of this presidency only if you’re a major investor in the stock market, a top corporate executive or a beneficiary of Trump’s largesse to his billionaire backers. But if you’re an average working American, you’re indubitably worse off. Hopefully, you’ll vote your economic interests on 3 November and deposit Trump’s congressional lapdogs into the dustbin of history. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

webTitle: Abortion rights group endorses Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Maine Senate race

fields.headline: Abortion rights group endorses Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Maine Senate race
fields.trailText: Reproductive Freedom for All – one of the country’s oldest pro-choice groups – backs Jackson in his fight against Republican Susan Collins
fields.bodyText: One of the oldest abortion rights groups in the US is endorsing Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine’s critical US Senate race, according to details first shared with the Guardian. Reproductive Freedom for All is supporting Jackson, the former state senate president, in challenging Susan Collins – the five‑term Republican incumbent who has been dogged on the campaign trail for her role in overturning abortion access in the US. Collins voted in 2018 to confirm conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court. In 2022, Kavanaugh joined the majority opinion overturning Roe v Wade, a landmark abortion rights protection. In the aftermath, more than a dozen states enacted near‑total abortion bans. This year’s midterm elections mark the first time Collins is on the ballot since the decision. “Flipping the Maine Senate race is a critical path to winning a Senate majority, and we do not restore a federal right to abortion without flipping the Senate majority,” said Mini Timmaraju, the group’s president. Timmaraju will join Jackson on Wednesday in Brunswick for the launch of the campaign’s Women for Troy coalition. Jackson, a former logger who began his political career as a Republican, once cast votes restricting abortion access before reversing course years later. He has expressed regret for his record and his earlier belief that abortion should “never be legal”. In a July interview with MS Now, Jackson said he recognized he had been “wrong”. “Early on, I wasn’t real clear on reproductive rights. But I had a lot of conversations over time. A lot of conversations with women, doctors, community members, just people that I came to trust,” he said. “And it became more and more clear to me that abortion access was healthcare.” Since 2017, Jackson has held a 100% rating from Planned Parenthood and has become one of Maine’s most consistently pro‑choice Democrats. In 2023, the year after the supreme court overturned Roe v Wade, he co‑sponsored legislation expanding abortion access to include medically necessary procedures after fetal viability. His evolution has extended beyond reproductive rights: Jackson has also shifted his positions on marriage equality and other social and economic issues, emerging as one of the Pine Tree State’s leading progressives during his time in the legislature. “[Jackson] in many ways reflects the reality of a majority of independents and Republicans in this country who now support abortion rights, but might personally have felt conflicted in the past,” Timmaraju told the Guardian. “Having someone like Troy in the Senate who can talk to his Republican colleagues and talk to some of those moderate Democratic colleagues who don’t have the same courage that he has is actually going to be a huge value add for our movement.” In June, Collins – who has long cast herself as a moderate Republican supportive of abortion access – said she did “not regret that vote” for Kavanaugh. Jackson’s campaign has seized on the remark to tie her to the Trump administration’s anti‑abortion agenda. “She can defend that vote all she wants. I’m running for Senate to restore and expand the federal right to abortion and make damn sure politicians never again get to take this freedom away from Mainers,” Jackson said in a statement. Planned Parenthood’s Super Pac announced this month it would spend more than $600,000 on ads criticizing Collins’s record on abortion in Maine. But strategists in both parties note that Collins’s seniority in Congress – and the millions of federal dollars she has steered back to Maine over the years – has historically proven difficult to beat. In a midterm shaped by record inflation, affordability concerns, and the military conflict with Iran, they argue her vote to confirm Kavanaugh may not be top of mind for many Mainers weighing their choices at the ballot box. Jackson – who mounted an unsuccessful bid for governor earlier this year – secured the Democratic nomination in July at a snap convention. He replaced Graham Platner, the oyster farmer who exited the race after facing allegations of sexual assault, which he denies. The turmoil around the race “gave us pause”, Timmaraju said, explaining the group’s decision to wait before endorsing Jackson. “We needed a little bit of time to regroup. We needed to follow the lead of people on the ground in Maine.”

webTitle: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael Behr

fields.headline: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition
fields.trailText: Everyone can see that the Iran war has been a strategic disaster for the US, while a failing president pretends he is winning, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
fields.bodyText: Now is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows. With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run. History will record the war against Iran as a turning point in the fortunes of the current US administration and a grievous wound to national prestige. Pumped with hubris after the audacious military operation to kidnap Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump believed an equally brisk triumph was available in the Middle East. The Tehran regime would be decapitated. The country’s hydrocarbon resources would then be available for US exploitation. Six months later, Iran is controlled by a new generation of hardliners. Emboldened by resilience under US and Israeli bombardment, they demand financial concessions from Washington as the price for peace – reparations and a right to toll the strait of Hormuz. The war is not over, it has just turned cold. Trump believes Iran’s fragile economy is close to collapse. He threatens to push it over the brink with “D-day” sanctions. The metaphor of second world war amphibious assault is supposed to make yet another round of financial coercion succeed where past embargos have failed. It is true that ordinary Iranians are suffering terrible privations, but repression limits their capacity to translate discontent into demands for political change. By contrast, US consumers, aggrieved by the inflationary consequences of the war, and confused about its purpose, get to express their unhappiness in midterm elections in November. The calculation in Tehran is that American tolerance for economic pain is low enough that Trump will be forced to blink first. It is a reasonable assumption: the need to declare mission accomplished to a domestic audience – even on terms that amount to defeat by any objective measure – drives an impatient president’s actions more than long-term strategy. If sanctions fail, diplomatic climbdown is the only remaining move. The Pentagon couldn’t revert to the all-out military option even if Trump ordered it, because Operation Epic Fury burned too much of the national munitions stockpile. This is where an asymmetry of cost and capability comes into play. Iran can frighten ships out of the Gulf with a few mines. It can harry neighbouring states with drones knocked together for less than $50,000 and dispatched from mobile launchers that are hard to target. The Patriot interceptors that protect US forces and their allies in the region cost $4-5m apiece. (More than 1,500 Patriots are thought have been fired in the war so far, leaving fewer than 830 in the US inventory.) That depletion has global repercussions, most pressingly in Ukraine where top-end US interceptors are essential for shielding civilians from Russia’s most sophisticated ballistic missiles. Trump’s attitude to that conflict has evolved from craven pro-Kremlin partisanship and an assumption of inevitable Russian victory to grudging respect for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s fortitude and ingenuity in proving that assumption wrong. But the shift is not stable. It depends on undertakings by Nato’s European members to cover the cost of arming Kyiv. If Trump had used normal diplomacy to cajole European democracies into financing the defence of their eastern flank, it would count as a foreign policy success – rebalancing the relationship to both sides’ benefit. But he did it with credulous admiration for Vladimir Putin and deranged demands for territory in Greenland. As a result, the European drive to autonomy looks less like burden-sharing and more like a hedge against American perfidy. It isn’t just Europe where US allies feel burned. Gulf states that found themselves on the frontline of Iranian retaliation in a war they didn’t start or want, expected a more reliable umbrella of protection. They feel unrewarded for their decades of service, hosting US military bases and functioning as proxies for American interests in the region. Last week Trump abruptly cut short a joint military exercise with South Korea – a loyal Asian partner to the US. A rational explanation, and the one preferred by Seoul, was that US forces were overstretched by their Middle Eastern entanglement. Trump framed it instead as an amicable gesture towards North Korean tyrant Kim Jong-un, whose regime he judged to be “unthreatening and respectful”. Such civility, lavished on a monstrous dictatorship, is withheld from Canada, a benign democracy. Trump dismisses his northern neighbour as an economic freeloader, barely even a proper country; a mislabelled territory that should be the 51st US state. Unsurprisingly, that attitude sours relations. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pulled out of trade talks last weekend, citing unreasonable last-minute demands from US negotiators. Trump responded with punitive tariffs, to which the Canadians promise “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation. The smaller economy is likely to suffer more from a trade war. But for Carney the cost in reduced commerce had to be weighed against the political damage he may incur if seen to capitulate to Trump’s bullying. He knows the US president takes concessions as an invitation to come back with yet more demands. He also knows that November’s midterm elections are likely to flip the House of Representatives to Democratic party control, and possibly the Senate too. Trump cannot be chastened by unwelcome election results. He would rather deny their validity. But irrefutable evidence of failure at the ballot box may at least stir some Republicans out of stupefied obedience to a commander-in-chief whose way of governing has made their party less popular and left their country friendless. Even if the constitutional mechanisms that are supposed to keep a president in check are only partly rehabilitated, the spell of impunity is broken. The cult of personality that once made Trump look like an irrepressible force of nature has shrunk to a sycophantic sect. An administration that styled itself as a national revolution looks more like a kleptocratic junta, using the privileges of office to pilfer what it can as the clock runs down. The president still has followers across the country. A hardcore bring unshakable devotion to the cause. But even some of them can surely sense the decay of purpose and whiff of panic in a man running out of ammunition. Trump’s reign is far from over. With his hands on the levers of American power he can still do a lot of damage. But the rest of the world has learned to read his lurches, anticipate his spasms, manoeuvre around him. The phase of deference is past. Now is the time of planning for whatever comes next in the dimming light of a waning star. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

webTitle: Wednesday briefing: How Canada has turned a trade dispute into a defence of its sovereignty

fields.headline: Wednesday briefing: How Canada has turned a trade dispute into a defence of its sovereignty
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: A collapsing trade deal has united Canadians more than ever, in an existential confrontation with the US president
fields.bodyText: Good morning. When the Guardian asked Canadian readers whether they planned to boycott US products after dramatic escalations in the ongoing DC/Ottawa trade war, we received more than 2,000 responses within 12 hours. This inundation is perhaps evidence of the existential crisis many Canadians feel they now face, something often lost in the granular reporting of trade negotiations: this is about so much more than the price of lumber. Assailed by a US president who has repeatedly expressed a desire to consume Canada into a supersized 51st state, the country has felt perpetually on the brink of war – albeit an economic one – since Donald Trump’s early second-term tariff salvo in February 2025. This culminated in Canada’s finance minister announcing tit-for-tat tariffs on key American industries yesterday, further incensing the US president. Canadian PM Mark Carney has emerged as a leader whose refusal to be dominated by Trump is underpinned by an ambition to reorder global politics. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to the Guardian’s Canada correspondent Leyland Cecco about trade narratives, Carney’s grand plan and the price of fruit in his local grocery store. But first, the headlines. Five big stories US news | Dolly Parton, one of the greatest singer-songwriters in country music who was also much cherished for her philanthropy, has died aged 80. UK news | UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience. UK politics | Andy Burnham will face an immediate test of his backing for electoral reform in his first week in parliament as prime minister, with almost 100 Labour MPs supporting a bid for a new national commission. Ukraine | A man from South Yorkshire is believed to be the first British citizen to die fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine. Climate crisis | The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed. In depth: ‘If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu’ The United States and Canada have enjoyed one of the strongest bilateral relationships in recent history. They share the longest unprotected border in the world, along with deep trading, security and cultural ties. But the second Trump presidency has brought about a fundamental breach in the shared values and understanding that once united the two nations. Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada, as he yearns to access its critical minerals. Carney, a former Governor of the Bank of England, was sworn in as prime minister last year in the midst of Trump’s tariff wars, having never held elected public office before. He has since become the first western leader to openly acknowledge the hazard Trump poses to the global order. In a high-profile January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, he urged “middle powers” like Canada to “act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.” Tariffs appear to have become a proxy for this political rupture. The ongoing US/Canada trade war began in February 2025, when Trump then (briefly) imposed tariffs of 25% on almost all imports from Canada and Mexico. Canada retaliated in kind, and the bitter dispute had just been rumbling on. Against this backdrop, Leyland tells me, reporters like him are “trying to figure out the magnitude of what’s happened.” *** What’s the latest? Last Tuesday, in a late night Truth Social post (is there any other kind?) Trump declared a “DEAL” with Canada was in its final stages. Trump delayed for three days the swingeing import taxes he was threatening to impose, which would have affected everything from anoraks to Christmas ornaments. The White House said in July that these 50% tariffs were in retaliation for “discriminatory treatment” by Canada. Still with me? On Friday, Canadian officials agreed a deal was still close, yet 24 hours later the whole thing fell apart. Canada walked out of negotiations hours before the 50% tariffs on roughly $20bn (£14.6bn) of Canadian goods kicked in on Saturday, with Carney accusing the US of using “economic integration as a weapon”. Yesterday, Canada pledged to roll out “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of US goods next month, prompting Trump to denounce the nation as “difficult and unreasonable”. Precisely how this all unravelled depends on whose narrative you follow. Carney’s position was that the US was breaching a red line on French language protection. Currently, Canadian rules require companies operating in Quebec, its predominantly Francophone province, to provide French-language goods and services to help protect its cultural identity. These stipulations have frustrated US negotiators. There’s also a counter narrative, that Canada’s negotiators were conceding so much – for example, accepting tariffs on the auto sector, steel and aluminium – that a number of senior Canadian politicians had urged Carney to harden his resolve. Meanwhile, US officials accused Canada of collapsing the deal by seeking additional last minute concessions. In the concurrent war of communications, Carney emerges the winner, says Leyland, “because he can defend the decision to walk way to Canadians”, while the US is hampered both by Trump’s ego and top officials pushing their own agendas. *** How Carney won this round Polling over the weekend found strong majority support for Carney’s stance in every Canadian province, and a mood of steadfast defiance can be read across Canada’s media. “The coming period will be hard and the damage may be awful but no one should ignore what is at stake. A free Canada is worth the sacrifice,” declared an editorial in the Globe and Mail. “What we see now is near uniform support for the prime minister ,” says Leyland, “and immense feelings of national unity”. This even extends to successionist Quebec, where support for independence from the rest of Canada is at its lowest level in decades. Carney – who has consolidated support for his previously ailing Liberals – is enjoying “a key political win” Leyland says, defending totemic language rights that are seen as integral to Canada’s cultural fabric. But his refusal to bow to US demands is part of a broader strategy. “What we’re seeing right now is the logical extension of that [Davos] speech, which was a warning and also laying the groundwork for how Canada would conduct itself”. For now, Carney is strengthening trade ties with China and the EU, to the chagrin of US negotiators. “The message is that Canada has long enjoyed a very beneficial relationship with the US and that’s over,” says Leyland. “Now we will walk away from the table if there is any erosion of our sovereignty.” Compare this Canadian unity with the domestic reaction south of the border: with the midterms looming, Trump is reportedly heading for a tariff-shaped clash with Senate Republicans. As venerable economist Paul Krugman pointed out yesterday: “The US is far more dependent on Canadian goods than most Americans realise.” *** The mood in Canada “There’s an asymmetric aim in this war,” says Leyland, “which is that Canada is fighting for its sovereignty, its national identity.” The US, meanwhile, is just “fighting for cheaper goods”. This perhaps explains why boycotting US goods has such visceral and consistent support among Canadians. A grassroots boycott has emerged as a consumer-driven response to the tariff war, with supermarket scanning apps like Maple Scan springing up to help users buy Canadian. Leyland is a parent of two young kids who like to eat berries – now he analyses every package in the grocery aisle to work out where they were grown. “I remember there was a period when US berries were on the steepest discount because they just weren’t selling.” And the decline of cross-border tourism has had a fairly devastating effect on American businesses. After Canadian visitor numbers fell by 26% in 2025, New York state launched a “NY loves Canada” promotional campaign this month to woo back its northern neighbours. “Every Canadian knows that this is not a fight that they want to be in”, says Leyland “but right now they believe it’s a fight worth having”. Weekend polling revealed a public who feel “frustrated”, “angry” and “exhausted” after 18 months of tariff turmoil. But, like their premier, they have no intention of backing down. Lesson: I need friends with deeper pockets. Sam Sport Football | Celtic threw away a four-goal lead in Austria as they missed out on the Champions League for the second year running. On Dolly Parton, the Sun and the Mirror both write “We will always love you, Dolly”, The Latest ‘Economic D-day’: How desperate is Trump to end Iran war? Once a mainstay of celebrations and rituals, passed down by ear, its continuity across the country’s regions was disrupted by war and migration, before the communist era brought a different, state-sanctioned version of folklore. But now, the music of the oberek, a traditional dance in which couples whirl around the dancefloor, is being reconfigured by a new generation of artists: the band Tercet Imperial weave traditional melodies and lyrics into contemporary production, replacing violins with synthesisers. webTitle: Dan Sullivan v Dan Sullivan: officials confirm challenger will join senator on Alaska midterms ballot

fields.headline: Dan Sullivan v Dan Sullivan: officials confirm challenger will join senator on Alaska midterms ballot
fields.trailText: The incumbent senator Dan S Sullivan has condemned ex-school teacher Dan J Sullivan, claiming he is running at the behest of Democrats to confuse supporters
fields.bodyText: Dan S Sullivan, the Republican senator, will be joined on the November ballot in Alaska by a challenger with a nearly identical name from the same party, election officials confirmed on Tuesday, adding a twist to what is expected to be one of the most hotly contested races of the midterms. The Republican senator is running for a third term against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former US House representative whom polls show is neck-and-neck with him in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 2008. Alaska holds nonpartisan primaries in which the top four vote-getters advance to the general election. The Associated Press reported that with 85% of the ballots counted, Dan J Sullivan, a retired school teacher and US Forest Service employee running as a Republican, would appear on the ballot alongside incumbent Dan S Sullivan and Peltola, with a fourth candidate yet to be announced. The other Sullivan entered the race earlier this year, with the incumbent senator condemning him as a “sham” candidate who is running at the behest of Democrats to confuse his supporters and split their votes. In June, Alaska election officials disqualified the other Sullivan from the election, but the state supreme court ordered him restored. The two were listed next to each other among the 16 candidates on primary ballots, but the senator had “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name, while his similarly named challenger was unadorned. It’s unclear how much of a threat the other Sullivan may pose to the senator’s chances of winning re-election. His 2.5% of the vote is much less than the more than 48% received by Peltola and almost 43% senator Sullivan won in last week’s primary. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for general elections for congressional offices, raising the possibility that residents who want to vote for the senator but are confused by the similar names can rank both, with their votes likely to wind up going to the incumbent. In addition to Alaska, Democratic leaders are seeking to win Senate seats from Republicans in North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Iowa, all of which voted for Donald Trump in 2024. They also hope to pick up a seat in blue state Maine, while defending Democratic-held seats in Michigan, Georgia and New Hampshire.

webTitle: Trump endorsement helps boost Darline Graham in South Carolina primary to replace her late brother in US Senate – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump endorsement helps boost Darline Graham in South Carolina primary to replace her late brother in US Senate – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve the remainder of her late brother Lindsey’s term, defeated congressman Ralph Norman in a South Carolina Republican Senate primary. Graham was endorsed by Donald Trump and won the primary run-off over Norman, despite a debate flub, by nearly 5 percentage points. Pennsylvania’s governor Josh Shapiro, told reporters that he was late for a news conference on the deadly measles outbreak in Lancaster county because he had been on the phone scolding the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, for “spreading misinformation” about vaccines. The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could be demolished if repairs are not carried out, Donald Trump’s administration warned in a court filing on Monday. Lawyers for the US president said the national arts complex in Washington DC must undergo a $250m renovation or risk facing the wrecking ball. Democrats asked a federal court in Washington DC to block Trump’s executive order to restrict mail voting on Tuesday, arguing that the US Postal Service does not have the legal authority it claims in a newly published change to its rules which would allow it to decide not to deliver ballots mailed by some voters. Canada said it will implement 50% retaliatory tariffs on $20bn worth of US goods – following through on prime minister Mark Carney’s vow to match Trump’s duties “dollar for dollar”. South Carolina’s population has increased by more than 700,000 residents over the last decade. That growth has fallen disproportionately in two areas of the state: the northern counties in congressman Ralph Norman’s district and the coastal communities of Horry County and its surrounding areas, represented by another Republican congressman, Russell Fry. The people moving into South Carolina tend to be Republicans. But they’re not South Carolina Republicans, at least not yet. The web of relationships that the state’s political culture trades on for support hasn’t caught up to many of them yet. South Carolina has no danger of turning purple, said Zachary Cogan of Lamar, a retired soldier and transplant from what he called the “communist” state of New York. “People who are coming here are, I would say 80-20 are red voters.” They’re not moving to South Carolina for its politics, he said. “That might have been a third or fourth tier reason for them to come here. They’re coming here because of lower taxes, a better standard of living from what they’re going to import from the North, lower housing costs and the ability to do more things with less government interference. Those are the priorities for people like me. It’s not necessarily the state’s politics, more than it’s what the state has to offer somebody who wants to move here.” Cogan was a Graham voter, he said. “Both candidates will be fine candidates for the Senate, either way,” Cogan said. “I’ve heard a lot of criticism for Darline Graham, that, well, she’s going to be learning by experience. But you know what? Maybe more of our representatives need to go into the fray untainted by prior politics.” Lindsey Graham’s long legacy in South Carolina has lingered beyond his death, influencing the vote for his sister Darline. “Probably the main reason I voted today: the bypass road here in Aynor is named after my father, and Mr. Lindsey Graham came the day of the dedication,” said Julius H. Goodson, Jr. of Aynor, South Carolina. “This is back in 2011. He came from Washington that morning for the dedication. It rained on the parade.” Aynor in the northeast corner of Horry County, is often forgotten by state leaders who focus on coastal development. Goodson, Aynor’s former fire chief, said he believed Graham had been different. Graham was a “$1 million man,” Goodson said. “When he made a million dollars in Washington, he said he had enough. He was working for the people. And I think his sister … I think she’ll be good for South Carolina.” The voters of the eastern corner of South Carolina proved decisive in the race to succeed the late senator Lindsey Graham in the Republican primary runoff on Tuesday. Horry County, home to Myrtle Beach, has grown tremendously over the last decade, and its Republican voting strength reflects it: it is likely to provide more than 10% of the state’s votes. As the votes were counted, the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, was running nearly three to one ahead of far-right congressman Ralph Norman there. Donald Trump visited Myrtle Beach on Friday to campaign for Graham. Voters appeared to respond. “Who is going to back Trump?” said Bill Bullard of Conway who voted Tuesday morning with his wife Linda. “Who is going to support Trump? It’s just that simple,” he said. They believed Graham had been undecided on her position on abortion, and would not have Trump’s leadership in office in the next presidency. The decision weighed heavily on their minds, he said. Trump’s endorsement mattered. Republican senator Tim Scott, who holds the other South Carolina seat, also weighed in with support for Graham, and that may have mattered more. “His endorsement mattered a lot. It was the changing factor. We think the world of Tim Scott.” Darline Graham, the sister of the late South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, has won a special Republican primary election to replace her brother on the November ballot for a full Senate term, according to an Associated Press projection. Graham, who was endorsed by Donald Trump and campaigned alongside the president in Myrtle Beach last week, defeated Ralph Norman, a congressman in the House Freedom Caucus, a group of right-wing Republicans. Graham led Norman 52% to 48%, or about 15,000 votes, with nearly 90% of the vote counted when AP made its call. The Republican Senate primary in South Carolina has dramatically tightened, with Darline Graham, the late Lindsey Graham’s sister, holding a narrow 52% – 48% lead over far-right congressman Ralph Norman, with 65% of the votes counted. The margin is currently close to 10,000 votes. Pennsylvania’s governor Josh Shapiro, told reporters on Tuesday that he was late for a news conference on the deadly measles outbreak in Lancaster county because he had been on the phone scolding the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, for “spreading misinformation” about vaccines. Kennedy, as we noted earlier, had visited Lancaster county in 2021 to deride vaccines in a region where an estimated 75% of Amish children are not vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella because of a conspiracy theory that the shot causes autism. The first two Pennsylvanians to die from measles in 35 years during the current outbreak were both unvaccinated residents of Lancaster county. “I’ve been sitting out in the parking lot talking to secretary Kennedy who reached out to me this morning, Shapiro said. “I was very very blunt with him and I made very clear that his actions, and the the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania, and that there’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation.” “There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions uh for our kids,” Shapiro added. “Sharing conspiracy theories and misinformation does not help the cause of public health and it leaves people less healthy and less safe and it leaves parents in a position where it’s harder for us to do our jobs to protect our children,” the governor said. The United States Capitol Police said they “seized a guillotine, which was spotted in the bed of a pickup truck” near the US Capitol on Tuesday. The police said in a press release, accompanied by photographs of the device, that they arrested the driver of the pickup truck “for Carrying a Dangerous Weapon for being in possession of the guillotine”. The suspect was identified as Philan-Tam-Duy Le, 35, of Julian, California. Democrats asked a federal court in Washington DC to block Donald Trump’s executive order to restrict mail voting on Tuesday, arguing that the US Postal Service (USPS) does not have the legal authority it claims in a newly published change to its rules which would allow it to decide not to deliver ballots mailed by voters whose eligibility it cannot confirm. The US supreme court ruled on Monday that a request to block the implementation of Trump’s March executive order from 23 states, and the District of Columbia, had been filed too early, since the USPS had not yet issued a change to its rules. In the suit, Democratic party officials, including the House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, and the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, claim that the new USPS rule, set to go into effect on Wednesday, is unlawful. “Today, we are taking strong, joint legal action to stop Trump’s unlawful attempt to restrict mail-in voting through the Postal Service. Yesterday’s Supreme Court ruling did not say that Trump’s executive order attacking voting rights is constitutional. In America, the law is clear: States have the authority to run elections - not the president,” the Democrats said in a statement. “We will not stand by while Trump and Republicans try to unnecessarily inject chaos and confusion into our elections, just weeks before voting begins. We are asking a district court to immediately stop the Trump administration from unlawfully disrupting mail-in voting in every state,” they added. The Democrats also asked the court to hear their motion for a preliminary injunction to block changes to mail voting on September 4, which is the day the midterm elections begin with the first absentee ballots sent to North Carolina voters. Polls have now closed in the Republican Senate primary in South Carolina, where voters were asked to replace their previous nominee, the late senator Lindsey Graham, with either his sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve the remainder of his term, of Ralph Norman, a congressman in the House Freedom Caucus, a group of right-wing Republicans. Graham, who was endorsed by Donald Trump but struggled on the debate stage, leads 56% – 44%, with about 2% of the vote counted, of just over 9,000 votes. Three former US presidents, Barack Obama, George W Bush and Bill Clinton, have added their voices, and those of their spouses, to the chorus of appreciation for the life of the late Dolly Parton. In a message posted on social media, Obama wrote: It’s hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton. Born in a one-room cabin, she earned 11 Grammys and an Emmy, built a business empire, helped millions of kids learn to read, and — as if that wasn’t enough — helped accelerate the research that led to the Moderna COVID vaccine. What a life. Michelle and I are thinking of Dolly’s family and her many, many fans. In a statement, Bush wrote: Laura and I, along with thousands of her fans, mourn the passing of Dolly Parton. We loved her music and her style. She was a great entertainer and even greater person. We respected her work to promote literacy, advance health, and strengthen communities. Dolly was a talented and hardworking American who will be missed. Clinton said in a social media post: Dolly Parton was one of a kind—a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart. She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from. And she always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy. Hillary and I were big fans and first saw her in 1974, and will always be grateful for the music and the memories. Our thoughts and prayers are with her family, her legion of fans, and everyone who loved her. Hillary Clinton said in a separate statement: Dolly Parton did all the good she could, for all the people she could, for as long as ever she could. From her legendary songwriting to the Imagination Library—which sent 1 million books a month to children across the country—she was the best of America. Dolly, we’ll miss your great heart. A federal appeals court on Tuesday sided with four Democrats running for Congress on Tuesday, by blocking the Federal ⁠Communications Commission from requiring television broadcasters to offer discounted advertising rates to political parties in the run-up to elections, a discount that currently only applies to candidates. A three-judge panel of the Richmond, Virginia-based 4th Circuit US Court of Appeals ruled 2-1 that campaign finance statutes “are clear that neither political parties nor joint fundraising committees with non-candidate members can be entitled” to the discounted rates mandated by the FCC. The Republican-controlled FCC had voted for a public notice that would allow party-controlled fundraising committees to get the discounted rates in the lead-up to midterm elections in ⁠November. Four Democratic candidates who sued to block the FCC ‌rule change: Jon Ossoff, a Georgia senator; Kristen McDonald Rivet, a Michigan ‌congresswoman; former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown, who is running to return to the Senate; and former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper, who is also running for a Senate seat. The FCC, the National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee argued thayt the court lacked jurisdiction to review the FCC notice. In June, the US supreme court struck down limits on how much party committees may spend in coordination with federal candidates but did not ‌address whether they could get the lower advertising rates. Since the Republican party has an enormous cash advantage over Democrats, the ruling, should it stay in place, would help to level the playing field in the broadcast ad war over the coming months. Democrat Ro Khanna, the Silicon Valley, California congressman widely believed to be considering a campaign for the presidency in 2028, argued on Tuesday that the US supreme court decision to allow Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail voting means that the court, “has completely lost its moral authority” and needs to be reformed. “We need to expand the court from 9 to 13 justices. We need to impose term limits on these justices. 18 years and you are out,” Khanna wrote in a social media post. The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could be demolished if repairs are not carried out, Donald Trump’s administration warned in a court filing on Monday. Lawyers for the US president said the national arts complex in Washington DC must undergo a $250m renovation or risk facing the wrecking ball. “Without those efforts, the ⁠Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” they argued. The warning came as Trump leaves a trail of destruction in Washington, demolishing the White House East Wing to make way for a $600m ballroom and ordering a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool that resulted in algae blooms and a peeling liner. The court filing represented the first time that Trump’s allies have raised the prospect of knocking down the Kennedy Center – a 100ft-high complex with a concert hall, opera house and theatre – as the dire alternative to closing it for two years of improvements. Such an aggressive move would be sure to face legal challenges, protests and an outcry from historic preservation groups. The threat emerged on Monday as the administration urged a federal judge to reject a fresh legal challenge to Trump’s efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center. The dispute has become part of a months-long battle over the president’s attempt to alter the memorial created by Congress in honour of John F Kennedy, the 35th US president who was assassinated in 1963. A federal judge ruled in May that only Congress has the power to change the Kennedy Center’s name. But the centre’s board, now largely made up of Trump appointees, voted 20-3 on 13 August to change the building’s signage to read: “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump.” It also voted to name the grounds the “President Donald J Trump Plaza”. As our colleague Jessica Glenza reports, the Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed on Tuesday that the both of the people who died from measles were unvaccinated residents of Lancaster County. Lancaster is the center of the current outbreak in Pennsylvania, and home to the largest population of Amish residents of any US county. The state health department reported in 2025 that while the overall rate of vaccination against measles, mumps and rubella for kindergarten children in Lancaster county was 90.5%, among the Amish population, the MMR vaccination rate there “was estimated to be around just 25%”. Lancaster country also happens to be where, in 2021, Robert F Kennedy, the anti-vaccine activist now serving as US health secretary, “spoke to a crowd of approximately 1,500, discussing topics of public health, personal freedom and the dangers of vaccines for profit”, according to The Lancaster Patriot, a far-right, local newspaper catering to the self-described “Plain People” community of Amish and Mennonite residents. During his hour-long speech, Kennedy made the discredited claim that the largely unvaccinated Amish does not suffer from autism, and suggested that there was a government conspiracy to force the community to be vaccinated. Speaking to the newspaper after his hour-long speech, Kennedy suggested that the push to get people to get vaccinated against Covid-19 was motivated by a desire “for money and control.” Canada has said it will implement 50% retaliatory tariffs on $20bn worth of US goods – following through on prime minister Mark Carney’s vow to match Donald Trump’s duties “dollar for dollar”. The list of products affected by Canada’s retaliatory tariffs includes a 50% duty on American steel and aluminum. There is also a 25% tariff on cheese, fish and seafood, as well as several wood products. Meanwhile, Trump has claimed that the US Navy has informed him that “all mines have been removed and/or detonated” from within the international waters of the strait of Hormuz. The US and Iran ‌have not exchanged air strikes for weeks, but attacks on vessels in the strait of Hormuz have continued as the two sides vie for control of the key maritime passage. It remains unclear how or when talks on ending the war between the two sides will resume. Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary, has defended the president’s policy to suspend higher tariffs on foreign beef imports to help mitigate prices for consumers. This comes amid growing criticism among the Republican ranks that the move threatens to hurt the growth of the US cattle industry, which is already facing tough herding conditions. “This is a very short-term fix from the president’s perspective, that he believed necessary to get lower cost beef on to American plates,” Rollins told Spectrum News. The president, and several lawmakers from both parties, have mourned the death of country music legend Dolly Parton. “This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. The president added that he would order American flags to be lowered to half-staff throughout the country for one week beginning Tuesday. And in South Carolina, voters will decide whether they want to establish a Graham family dynasty as they go to the polls today in a Republican run off election, pitting Darline Graham against US Representative Ralph Norman. Trump has endorsed Graham and held a rally for her on Friday in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, The primary election will be another in a series of tests of Trump’s sway with voters in this year’s midterm elections. The primary will decide whether the current Senator Graham or Norman will ⁠be the Republican nominee in the November election. John Fetterman, a Democratic senator from Pennsylvania who frequently breaks with his party and votes with Republicans, has seen his approval rating drop with Democrats over the last two years, while gaining popularity with the state GOP, according to a New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll. Fetterman was the sole Democrat to vote no on several war powers resolutions to curb the Trump administration’s military action in Iran. Earlier this year, he voted to confirm Trump’s pick to lead the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Markwayne Mullin, and last year Fetterman routinely joined Republicans on key votes to keep the government open – while Senate Democrats withheld support for key appopriations bills to protest expiring Affordable Care Act subsidies. New polling shows that while 74% of Democrats in the Keystone state had a favorable opinion of Fetterman in 2024 – two years after he won his Senate election – by 2026 that has fallen to 22%. Meanwhile, only 25 % of Pennsylvania Repbublicans viewed Fetterman favorably in 2024. That number has shot up to 73%. Despite not confirming whether he would seek a second term in office, Fetterman recently said that he has no intention to switch parties. He has, however, issued a caveat – he would consider leaving the Democratic caucus if it became the “anti-Israel party”. Fetterman has emerged as one of Israel’s most prominent advocates among Senate Democrats, even as others in the party back away from their traditional support for the country amid accusations that prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government committed genocide in Gaza. Donald Trump has reacted to the news that country music legend Dolly Parton has died. “This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” the president wrote on Truth Social. Trump said he would order American flags to lowered to half-staff throughout the country for one week beginning Tuesday. A number of US lawmakers from both parties honored Parton in tribute posts. Marsha Blackburn, a Republican senator from Parton’s home state of Tennessee, said that the singer-songwriter’s death “leaves a void that no one can ever fill. Dolly, we will always love you”. Meanwhile, Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, noted that Parton “was not only a talented musician” but also “a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief”. He added: “Her music and humanity touched millions. She will be sorely missed.” Follow along at our dedicated blog here: While we’ll be keeping an eye on the results of the South Carolina run off election today, that will determine the Republican nominee for the US Senate race, another contest that will test the strength of Donald Trump’s endorsement powers is happening in deep-red Oklahoma. Here, a run off competition to be the Republican gubernatorial nominee is playing out. Trump’s pick – former state lawmaker and businessman Mike Mizzei – is up against Oklahoma attorney general Gentner Drummond. The initial June primary saw Mizzei trailing Drummond by less than a single point – with neither receiving a majority of the vote. Whichever Republican secures the nomination, they are all but certain to clinch the overall victory in November over the Oklahoma House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson. No Democrat has won the governor’s race since in twenty years. Drummond, for his part, has received the ire of the president after he filed a lawsuit to block construction of a $4bn aluminium smelter factory in Inola, Oklahoma. Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary, has defended the president’s policy to suspend higher tariffs on foreign beef imports to help mitigate prices for consumers. This comes amid growing criticism among the Republican ranks that the move threatens to hurt the growth of the US cattle industry, which is already facing tough herding conditions. “This is a very short-term fix from the president’s perspective, that he believed necessary to get lower cost beef on to American plates,” Rollins told Spectrum News. However, the agriculture secretary said that she did not yet know where the beef would be imported from, noting that it was part of US trade representative Jamieson Greer’s remit. “I am actually not part of any of those conversations, so I am not sure what that looks like. I think we’ll know very soon,” Rollins said. As we’ve been reporting, Canada today pledged to roll out “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of US goods next month, days after Donald Trump’s 50% tariffs on roughly $20bn of Canadian goods, ranging from honey to hockey sticks, took effect. Ottawa has released a list of more than 700 targets on goods ranging from fish and cheese to smartphones and steel imported from the United States. The new tariffs on these products will carry rates of 15%, 25% or 50%. Canada’s tariffs on many US products would double from 25% to 50%, with the largest share of the new measures affecting steel and aluminum. Some of the many US items Canada is now targeting include: 1.
